The smell hits me first, sharp and metallic, like copper left out in the rain. It's the scent of ozone and burnt insulation, clinging to the back of my throat. My skin prickles, a sudden, involuntary shiver running down my spine as if the air itself has changed pressure. I close my eyes, trying to anchor the sensation, but the memory resists, bleeding into a haze of distorted light and shadow.

I am standing in a neighborhood where the streetlights were installed over a century ago in the old cotton fields. They are old, dusty motors in metal cases with handles, standing behind locked doors. I walk past an electric line, my hand brushing the cool, rough wire. Suddenly, the light turns a sickly green. A knock rattles at the door, then it slams shut behind me. The streetlights flare on, the traffic lights stubbornly stay green, and I step on the cord. The world goes dark.

The whole neighborhood panics. There is a brilliant blink, a flash so white it hurts, followed by a whistling sound. It is a high, thin shriek that cuts through the silence, a sound that sent a shockwave through the air. I never see a person. No faces, no bodies, just the sound and the heat. My house is dark in that same moment because I never saw my parents. They are gone, erased by the event, leaving only the sensory residue.

The streetlights go off again, the traffic lights remain green, and my breath comes back to me. My body stops sweating, goes dark for a moment, waiting for the next signal. This event was never recorded, never even filmed. I am the only witness who saw it happen, not a clerk who recorded it. The fact that it happened is evidence that it happened, not a statement about the event. The evidence is the sound, the light, the heat, and the strange, whistling-like sound. That's the whole story.

I remember the geography of that night as a tangled travel plan, a long winding route along the ancient walled city edges that flows north to south. I was trying to read the wall from one story, a ship of the city walls, trying to find the shortcut through the Automatic Reactors district. The trick was to take the longest-magnified route up north to south, then go east to west through the reactors, then come back and read what happened where the reactors were. Two things I was building on the trip, one a memory, the other a diary.

I should give you the second-travel-diary. That's the shortcut, the only way the whole thing's ever actually happened. Name the thing first, and I'll always remember it. Name the thing, and the thing will remember. The sound was the evidence, the proof that something had happened. It was a moment of pure, unfiltered memory, a snapshot of a city that had long since forgotten its past. The sound was the evidence, the proof that something had happened.
